items.title: Canonical group-sequential alpha-spending design
items.statement: Fix a finite integer maximum K≥1, prescheduled information fractions 0<t_1<⋯<t_K=1 with t_j the fraction of total planned information at look j, and α∈(0,1). A spending function is a nondecreasing A:[0,1]→[0,α] with A(0)=0 and A(1)=α. Under the stipulated simple null P_0, the standardized vector Z has law N_K(0,Σ), with Σ_jk=√(t_j/t_k) for j≤k and symmetry otherwise. The covariance is justified locally. One-sided upper and symmetric two-sided designs stop at the first crossing; cumulative null rejection probability through look k is the union probability of the corresponding crossing events. Exact calibration means that this probability is A(t_k) at every look. In an experiment with a nonempty alternative and singleton null, this probability is the test size.

references.title: David L. DeMets and K. K. Gordon Lan, Interim Analysis: The Alpha Spending Function Approach, Statistics in Medicine 13 (1994), PDF pp. 2–3, 6–7
Michael J. Grayling, James M. S. Wason, and Adrian P. Mander, Group Sequential Clinical Trial Designs for Normally Distributed Outcome Variables, The Stata Journal 18(2) (2018), PDF pp. 2–4
Giorgos Minas, Multivariate Global Testing and Adaptive Designs, PhD thesis, Chapter 5 §§5.3–5.3.1, printed pp. 72–73

items.title: Recursive group-sequential boundary calibration
items.statement: Given the Axiom of Choice and a canonical design, set t_0=0 and R_0=empty. For k=1,…,K, if A(t_k)=A(t_{k−1}), set the look-k boundary to +infinity. Otherwise, in the one-sided mode choose the unique real b_k satisfying P_0(R_{k−1} union {Z_k>=b_k})=A(t_k); in the symmetric two-sided mode choose the unique c_k>=0 satisfying P_0(R_{k−1} union {|Z_k|>=c_k})=A(t_k). Set R_k to the resulting union of crossing events and output the K boundaries. The procedure uses exact probabilities under the stipulated joint null law; it makes no claim about a particular numerical integration routine.

items.title: Group-sequential boundaries exist uniquely and spend alpha exactly
items.statement: Assume AC and the canonical design. The recursive algorithm is well-defined: each positive spending increment has a unique finite boundary and each flat increment has boundary +infinity. Under P_0, rejection by look k has probability A(t_k), so the terminal simple-null rejection probability is alpha. In any embedding with a nonempty alternative and singleton null whose law is P_0, the test size is alpha. The same cumulative probability identity holds for separately calibrated symmetric two-sided crossings. The result is conditional on the specified joint Gaussian null law and prescheduled information fractions; it gives no guarantee for data-dependent timing, estimated variance, or an unspecified composite null.
items.strategy: Factor the canonical covariance as an invertible lower-triangular Gram matrix. The resulting nondegenerate Gaussian law has full support and atomless standard-normal marginals. For each look, the probability of a new crossing is a continuous strictly decreasing function of the boundary, with endpoint values equal to the previous cumulative spend and one. The intermediate value theorem gives the unique boundary; the recursion then gives the spending identities.

items.title: Two-look Pocock-type symmetric spending
items.statement: With alpha=0.05 and t_1=1/2,t_2=1, the Pocock-type spending curve A_P(t)=alpha log(1+(e−1)t) has first spend a_1=alpha log((1+e)/2). If Phi is the standard normal CDF and q(u) its unique u-quantile, the first symmetric boundary is c_1=q(1−a_1/2). The final symmetric boundary c_2 is the unique solution of P_0(|Z_1|>=c_1 or |Z_2|>=c_2)=alpha; the canonical correlation is 1/sqrt(2).
items.strategy: Check the named spending curve, construct its standard-normal quantile, and use the calibration theorem for the exact correlated two-sided final boundary.

items.title: Two-look O’Brien–Fleming-type spending
items.statement: With alpha=0.05 and t_1=1/2,t_2=1, the two-sided O’Brien–Fleming-type curve A_OF(0)=0, A_OF(t)=2[1−Phi(z_{0.975}/sqrt(t))] for t>0 has first spend a_1=2[1−Phi(z_{0.975}sqrt(2))]. The first symmetric boundary is c_1=z_{1−a_1/2}; the final boundary c_2 is the unique solution of P_0(|Z_1|>=c_1 or |Z_2|>=c_2)=0.05, with canonical correlation 1/sqrt(2).
items.strategy: Check the two-sided O’Brien–Fleming spending curve, solve the first-look symmetric tail equation, and leave the final boundary as the exact unique bivariate-normal calibration root.
